Female Eastern long-fingered bats give birth to a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter], a reproductive strategy that maximizes investment in each offspring rather than litter size. Under the stable thermal conditions of maternity roosts, which average 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C], the gestation period proceeds for approximately 60 days [tg = approximately 60 days], during which the gestating embryo develops within a tightly regulated uterine environment. This prolonged gestation is typical of temperate-zone Myotis species and reflects the energetic constraints imposed by seasonal insect availability. The single-pup strategy, combined with a relatively short gestation relative to the total annual cycle, limits the maximum annual reproductive rate to one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year], a value that aligns well with the slow life-history pace of many cave-roosting vespertilionids. Field observations consistently confirm that females rarely produce more than one successful litter annually, even under favorable conditions.

At parturition, female neonates emerge at a wet weight of approximately 2.842 grams [Wwb = approximately 2.842 grams], a modest mass that represents roughly 31.6 percent of the pup's eventual adult body weight. This initial size is consistent with the altricial developmental mode typical of the genus, where newborns are hairless and entirely dependent on maternal care for thermoregulation and nutrition. The birth mass has been recorded across multiple field seasons in Japanese populations and shows relatively low interannual variation, suggesting strong canalization during organogenesis. The relatively small body size at birth imposes significant energetic demands on the lactating female, who must provision the nursing offspring during a period of high basal maintenance requirements. Comparisons with sympatric congeners such as Myotis daubentonii reveal that Myotis macrodactylus neonates are slightly heavier when corrected for adult body size, a pattern that may be linked to the relatively long gestation period.

The ultimate wet weight attained by adult females in this species reaches approximately 9 grams [Wwi = approximately 9 grams], placing Myotis macrodactylus among the smaller-bodied members of the eastern Palearctic bat community. This adult mass is achieved several weeks after weaning, during a period of rapid mass gain fueled by the seasonal abundance of dipteran and lepidopteran prey. Body size in this species shows modest geographic variation, with individuals from northern Hokkaido populations averaging slightly larger than those from Honshu, consistent with Bergmann's rule applied to endotherms. The 9-gram upper mass limit is maintained throughout the active season, although females entering hibernation in autumn may increase body mass through fat deposition to around 10.5 to 11 grams, reflecting substantial preparation for winter torpor. This ability to accumulate energy reserves is critical for overwinter survival, as lactating females often enter the pre-hibernation period depleted from the energetic costs of reproduction.

The maximum lifespan recorded for wild individuals of Myotis macrodactylus extends to 34 years [am = 34 years] under the thermal conditions typical of summer maternity colonies, which are maintained at 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C] during the active season. This extreme longevity is among the highest documented for any mammal of its body size, underscored by field recapture data from banding studies conducted in Nagano Prefecture, where one female was captured 34 years after initial marking. Such extended lifespan is characteristic of the genus Myotis, whose members are known for exceptionally slow senescence rates relative to other small-bodied mammals. The long life expectancy is coupled with delayed reproductive maturation, with females typically producing their first litter at 365 days since birth [tp = 365 days since birth] at a temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. This combination of slow development and extended lifespan represents a classic bet-hedging strategy in a temperate environment where reproductive success can be highly variable from year to year.

The weaning period in Myotis macrodactylus concludes at approximately 45 days [tx = approximately 45 days] under the stable microclimate of the maternity roost, which again averages 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. This duration aligns closely with the weaning times reported for other temperate cave-roosting bats such as Myotis myotis and Myotis lucifugus. The age at weaning marks a critical transition, as the juvenile must now meet its daily metabolic costs entirely through foraging success rather than maternal milk. Comparative data suggest that weaning age is relatively invariable across the genus, likely due to the fixed developmental requirements for wing growth and aerodynamic competence before independent flight is possible. The post-weaning period, extending through the first autumn, is characterized by high juvenile mortality, often exceeding 50 percent in the first year, as inexperienced foragers struggle to accumulate sufficient fat reserves for hibernation.
